title: Search inside an analytics tool
excerpt: When navigation misses, search should return the metric, customer, or saved view in the operator's words, inside their scope, with a way back to a number they can cite.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall, connecting a name to the screen it belongs on.
caption: The string is a path back to the right screen. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should analytics search return first?
faqs.answer: The metric, the customer, or the saved view they named, with the scope on the row. Rank those above help articles. Group by kind so a customer named Activation does not outrank the activation metric. Recent items should appear when the box is focused and still empty.

faqs.question: How should search treat data outside someone's scope?
faqs.answer: Omit customers they cannot open. For a metric, a locked row with a reason is usually kinder than a silence that implies you do not track it. Repeat the scope on the box, so an empty result is not mistaken for a missing customer.

faqs.question: Should operators and analysts share one search box?
faqs.answer: No. Event and column search is a different job, with a different permission and a different empty state. A result should become a citable metric only after a definition is published. Until then it stays out of the operator's search.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Operators reach for analytics tool search ux when the dashboards, the nav, and the pinned number have not taken them to the thing they need. Show matches in their language, and show a way back to a figure they can cite.

Nielsen Norman Group's work on how long people stay notes that visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that they read only about a quarter of the text on a page they do open. Search results have to be the match, scannable in a glance, not a paragraph about how search works.

## What an operator types

They type a metric, a customer, a campaign, a teammate's view, or a word from a definition. "Activation." "Northwind." "The Monday board." "Refund rate." They are trying to recover a number they have seen before, or check whether a thing they can name is inside the tool at all.

They also type dates and slang. "Last quarter." "Churn." "MRR." Your search has to know the nouns you used on the charts. If the chart says "paid invoices" and they search "revenue," either return that chart and say why it matched, or teach the synonym on the metric itself so the next search is unnecessary. A glossary that lives in a help center will not be opened. A line under the result will.

Do not make search the way a new person finds the pinned number. That number is the first screen. Search is for the second question, and for the day the nav was reorganized and muscle memory failed. If the only path to "paid invoices" is the box, the information architecture is unfinished. Fix the nav, and keep search.

## Results a person can scan

Lead with the object, then the kind, then the scope. "Paid invoices · metric · company, last 7 days." "Northwind · customer · EU shop." "Monday board · saved view · private to Sam." The matched word is in the title. A highlight buried in a description will be missed, because they will not read the description.

Rank metrics and saved views above help articles. Rank a customer above a dashboard that merely mentions the customer in a footnote. Rank a view they can open above a view they cannot, or mark the locked one so they do not click into a blank. The job is to get back to a citable figure. Documentation is a different job, and it can sit in a separate group under the real objects.

When the box is focused and empty, show recent metrics and recent customers for this person. Recent items teach the shape of a row. They also rescue the operator who remembers that they looked at something yesterday and cannot remember the name you gave it. "Paid invoices" and "Net collected" are easy to swap in memory. Recents are the undo.

Group the results by kind when several kinds match. Metrics, then customers, then views. A flat list sorted by text score will put a customer named Activation above the activation metric, which is a bad joke the first time and a broken tool the second. Kind is a stronger signal than string overlap. Use it.

## Scope is part of the match

Search has to obey the same permissions as the charts. If this operator cannot see the US shop, a search for a US customer should not reveal that the customer exists, unless your policy is to show a locked row. Pick one and write it down. For customer data, omitting is usually the safer default. For metrics, a locked row with a reason is kinder, because the metric's existence is not a secret. "Margin · limited to finance" tells the truth. A missing margin metric makes them think you do not track it.

Say when a filter is narrowing search. If they are scoped to the EU shop, the box should repeat that. "Searching inside the EU shop." Otherwise an empty result for a real customer looks like a defect. Offer "ask an owner" only if an owner can actually help, and only when the name might exist outside their scope. Do not offer it on every empty state or it becomes noise.

A saved view they can see should show its filters in the result, in short form. "EU, last quarter, paid invoices." Opening it should not feel like teleporting. Leave the query in the box and a way back to the results. If the view's number fails to load, that is an error with its own sentence, not a reason to clear the search.

## Empty, close, and wrong

Empty needs the query and the scope in the sentence. "Nothing in the EU shop matches 'northwind.' Check the spelling, or clear the shop scope if you can." If they cannot clear the scope, do not tell them to. Tell them what they may try instead: a different spelling, a metric name, a view.

Close matches should be offered, not swapped. "No metric named churn. There is a metric named canceled accounts." Let them choose. Silent substitution that drops them on a neighboring KPI is how the wrong number gets quoted.

Wrong kind is its own empty. They searched a customer inside a metric index, or the reverse. If you can tell, say so. "No customer named 'activation.' There is a metric with that name." The way back is the other group of results, already open, not a new search they have to invent.

Keep a path out that is not the box. A link to their pinned number, and a link to the list of metrics, should sit with the results. Search repairs navigation. A product that offers no list at all will be searched for everything, including things a list of twelve would have solved. If you have fewer than twenty metrics, show the list. Use search as the type-ahead on that list, not as a separate world.

## Speed and what you index

The result should arrive while they still remember why they typed. Keep them on the page. A full navigation to a search screen that forgets the chart they were on is a way to get lost twice. A panel over the current view, with the same type and the same definitions, is enough. Motion can bring the panel in. The wait, if there is one, should be a quiet mark on the box, not a skeleton that replaces the number they already trusted.

Index the names you are willing to say in a meeting: metric titles, definition sentences, customer names you are allowed to show this role, saved view titles, and the people who own a view. Do not index the contents of private notes into a company-wide search. Do not index raw event payloads. Search is not a backdoor to the warehouse. If an analyst needs that, it is a different tool with a different permission, and it should look different so nobody confuses the two.

Tell them, in one line under the box, what this search covers. "Metrics, customers in your scope, and views you can open." That sentence prevents a week of bug reports from someone who typed a column name from a CSV. When you add a kind, update the line. The line is the contract.

## The warehouse is a different box

Some analysts need to search events, columns, and raw rows. That is a real job, and it is not the operator's search. Give it a different place, a different empty state, and a different permission. If you put it behind the same box, every operator will eventually run a query they do not understand and pin the result next to a trusted metric. The homepage number will then have a cousin that does not match, and the argument will be about your tool.

Name the analyst box for what it is. "Event search, not the metrics your team cites." Require the published definition when an analyst wants a result to become a metric. Until then, the result stays in their workspace and does not appear in the operator's search. This is a settings and permissions decision showing up inside search, and it is worth the extra sentence. One box that tries to be both a glossary and a database console will be distrusted by both audiences.

Operators who never see that second box should not be told it exists in the empty state of the first. Their empty state offers synonyms, scope, and recent metrics. The analyst's empty state offers tables and fields. Different sentences, because the jobs are different.

## Review five queries

Use five real ones. The metric everyone nicknames. A customer in scope. A customer out of scope. A teammate's view. A word that appears only in a definition. If the nickname fails, add the synonym to the metric. If the out-of-scope customer leaks, stop and fix that before you tune ranking. If the definition word matches ten metrics, show the definition snippet only for the top few, not a wall of paragraphs. They will not read a quarter of it.

Settings are the other escape hatch, when the number is wrong because a source, a definition, or a pinned metric needs to change. [Settings in an analytics tool](/blog/settings-in-an-analytics-tool) is the next piece: a cabinet for those changes, not a second product hiding behind the search box.

If your operators still export a spreadsheet because they cannot find the figure they trust, look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Notice which interfaces put the object in the open. Then list the five queries you want the box to answer, and which of them should never have needed search.
